key_terms.meaning: Energy stored in an elastic body by the work its own deformation absorbs; for a linear spring U = ½P Δ, units joule (J)
U = P²L/(2AE) for a bar of force P, length L, area A, modulus E
U = ∫ M²/(2EI) dx over the beam length; EI is flexural rigidity
U = T²L/(2GJ) for constant torque T, shear modulus G, polar second moment J
Δ = ∂U/∂P: the partial derivative of strain energy with respect to a load gives the displacement at that load along its line; ∂U/∂M gives the rotation
A fictitious load Q applied at a point where no real load acts, so that ∂U/∂Q gives the deflection there; set Q = 0 after differentiating
External virtual work equals internal virtual work: 1·Δ = Σ (n·δL) for any self-consistent virtual force system
Truss deflection Δ = Σ nNL/(AE), where N is the real member force and n the member force from a load of 1 at the point, in the direction wanted
For a plane truss, m + r − 2j; m members, r reaction components, j joints; zero means determinate
A member beyond the minimum needed for stability; its force cannot be found from joint equilibrium alone
Solve each joint in turn using ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0; start at a joint with at most two unknown member forces
Δ = ∫ Mm/(EI) dx, with M real bending moment and m moment due to a unit load at the point and direction wanted
An equation stating that a displacement at a released point must equal a known value, usually zero when a support is restored
The extra reaction removed to make the structure determinate; its value is then found from compatibility
M₁L₁ + 2M₂(L₁+L₂) + M₃L₂ = −6A₁x̄₁/L₁ − 6A₂x̄₂/L₂ for constant EI; A is area of the free bending moment diagram, x̄ its centroid distance
Bending moment at a support of a fully clamped span under given load; it is the starting value in moment distribution
DF = k/Σk at a joint, where k = 4EI/L for a member with a fixed far end and 3EI/L for a pinned far end; shares the unbalanced moment among the members meeting there
Fraction of a distributed moment carried to the far end of the same member: ½ if the far end is fixed, 0 if it is pinned
For a redundant force X, ∂U/∂X = 0: the strain energy is a minimum at the true value, which is the compatibility condition
A section where the bending moment changes sign, between a hogging support region and a sagging span region

takeaways: A linear elastic member stores half the product of final load and deflection, U = ½PΔ, because the load grows from zero.
Each loading type has one closed form: P²L/(2AE) for axial, ∫M²dx/(2EI) for bending, T²L/(2GJ) for torsion; they add for a member that carries several.
Castigliano turns the derivative of energy into a deflection; a dummy load is set to zero only after differentiating.
The unit load method is Castigliano with the derivative taken first: ∂M/∂P is the unit-load moment m.
For a truss the unit load integral is a sum over members, Σ nNL/(AE); for a beam it is ∫Mm dx/(EI), split wherever EI or the moment law changes.
Indeterminacy is not a dead end: remove a redundant, find the gap it leaves, and force the gap to close, by compatibility or by least work.
Propped cantilever: R = 3wL/8, fixing moment wL²/8, peak sagging only 9wL²/128 because the fixing moment acts on every section.
The three-moment equation links support moments span pair by span pair; moment distribution balances joint by joint and is the better hand method for four spans or more.
bank_note: Long answers derive the energy expression first, then apply it to a truss or beam with a labelled diagram, a table of member forces or moments, consistent units, and a closing check by a second method.

bank.q: Define strain energy for a linearly elastic body. Derive the expression for strain energy stored in a uniform bar under axial load, and show that it equals half the product of load and extension.
outline: Define U as the work done by a gradually applied load, stored and recovered on unloading
Load-extension line is straight, so work = area of a triangle = ½PΔ
Use Δ = PL/(AE) and substitute to get U = P²L/(2AE)
Units: joule
Per unit volume σ²/(2E); worked number for a strut
answer: Definition. When a load is applied gradually to an elastic body, the body deforms and the load does work. That work is stored in the material as strain energy U and is given back in full when the load is removed. Its unit is the joule, 1 J = 1 N·m.

The work is a triangle. In a linearly elastic bar the extension grows in proportion to the load. At an intermediate load p the extension is δ, and a small increase dδ needs work p dδ. Adding these from zero to the final load P and extension Δ gives the area under the straight load-extension line:

answer.pre: U = ∫ p dδ, from δ = 0 to Δ, = area of triangle = ½ × P × Δ

answer: The ½ appears because the load rises from zero to P, so the average load during stretching is P/2.
Substituting the extension. A uniform bar of length L, area A and modulus E stretches by Δ = PL/(AE). Then

answer.pre: U = ½ P × PL/(AE) = P²L/(2AE)

answer: Check of units: N² × m/(m² × N/m²) = N·m = J.

Per unit volume. With σ = P/A and ε = σ/E, U = ½ × (σA)(εL) = (σ²/2E) × AL. The energy per unit volume is σ²/(2E); at the yield stress it is the modulus of resilience, and the total at yield is the proof resilience.

answer.text: Worked number. An aluminium strut: L = 1.2 m, A = 250 mm², E = 70 GPa, P = 20 kN.

answer: Points to remember. U is a scalar and never negative. It grows as P², so doubling the load stores four times the energy, and energies from separate load cases do not simply add. A load of the same size applied suddenly gives twice the extension and four times this energy.
Closing check. Three routes, ½PΔ, P²L/(2AE) and σ²/(2E) × volume, all give 13.71 J for the strut, which confirms U = ½PΔ = P²L/(2AE).

bank.q: State Castigliano’s theorem for displacement of a linear elastic structure. Explain the condition under which it is valid and how a dummy load is used to find deflection at a point with no load.
outline: State Δ = ∂U/∂P along the line of action of P, and θ = ∂U/∂M
Valid for linear elastic behaviour, small deflections, rigid supports, no temperature strain
Write U for all loads, differentiate with respect to one
Dummy load Q: include, differentiate, then set Q = 0
Worked number: cantilever tip deflection
answer: Statement. For a linearly elastic structure carrying loads P₁, P₂, …, the partial derivative of the total strain energy with respect to one load gives the displacement of that load’s point along its line of action:

answer.pre: Δᵢ = ∂U/∂Pᵢ        θᵢ = ∂U/∂Mᵢ

answer: The second form gives the rotation where a moment Mᵢ acts. This is Castigliano’s second theorem.
Why it works. For a single load on a linear member U = ½PΔ and Δ = P/k, so U = P²/(2k) and dU/dP = P/k = Δ. With several loads, increasing one load by dPᵢ adds work Δᵢ dPᵢ, the extra energy.

Conditions. (1) The material obeys Hooke’s law, so U is quadratic in the loads. (2) Deflections are small, so the geometry does not change. (3) Supports do not yield. (4) No temperature strain or lack of fit; those need extra terms. For a rubber cord or a buckling column, ∂U/∂P is not the deflection.
Dummy load. Where no load acts at the wanted point:

answer.pre:
1. Add a fictitious load Q there, along the wanted deflection
   (a fictitious moment for a rotation).
2. Write M or N with Q kept as a symbol.
3. Differentiate: Δ = ∫ M (∂M/∂Q) dx/(EI) or Σ N (∂N/∂Q) L/(AE).
4. Only now set Q = 0.

answer: If Q = 0 is put in before differentiating, U no longer depends on Q and the derivative is zero.

answer.text: Worked number 1, real load. Steel cantilever, L = 2 m, EI = 200 × 10⁹ × 8 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.6 × 10⁶ N·m², tip load P = 1 kN. With x from the free end, M = Px:
Worked number 2, dummy load. A 3 m cantilever with w = 4 kN/m and EI = 2400 kN·m² has no tip load. Add Q at the tip: M = wx²/2 + Qx, ∂M/∂Q = x.

answer: Closing check. Both answers match the standard results PL³/(3EI) and wL⁴/(8EI), so the theorem and the dummy-load step are applied correctly.

bank.q: State the principle of virtual work for deformable bodies and use it to derive the unit load formula for deflection of a pin-jointed truss.
outline: Virtual force system in equilibrium, real displacements compatible
External virtual work = 1 × Δ
Internal virtual work = Σ n × (member extension), extension = NL/(AE)
Equate: Δ = Σ nNL/(AE)
Sign convention and a worked number
answer: Principle. Take a deformable body in equilibrium under a set of forces (the virtual force system) and give it any small, compatible set of displacements (here the real ones). Then the work done by the external virtual forces through the real displacements equals the work done by the internal virtual forces through the real deformations:

answer.pre: external virtual work = internal virtual work

answer: The two systems are independent: the forces need only be in equilibrium, the displacements need only fit together.

Choosing the virtual system. To find the deflection Δ of joint J in a chosen direction, apply a single load of 1 at J in that direction and nothing else. Solve the truss for the member forces n it causes. These forces are in equilibrium with the unit load.

External work. The unit load rides through the real deflection Δ of J, so the external virtual work is 1 × Δ. The support reactions of the virtual system do no work because the real supports do not move.
Internal work. Each member carries the virtual force n and really stretches by e = NL/(AE), where N is its real force. The internal virtual work in that member is n × e.

answer.text: Result. Equating and summing over all members:
answer.pre: 1 × Δ = Σ n × NL/(AE)     so     Δ = Σ nNL/(AE)

answer: Tension is positive for both N and n. A positive Δ is in the direction of the unit load; a negative answer means the joint moves the other way. A member whose length changes for another reason (temperature, lack of fit) uses that change in place of NL/(AE).

answer.text: Worked number. Two bars AC and BC with pins A and B 2 m apart and apex C 1.5 m up; each bar 1.8028 m long, A = 200 mm², E = 70 GPa, 10 kN down at C. The sine of each bar’s angle is 1.5/1.8028 = 0.8321.

answer: Closing check. Castigliano gives the same: N = −0.6009P, ∂N/∂P = −0.6009, and 2 × (−6009)(−0.6009)(1.8028)/(1.4 × 10⁷) = 0.93 mm.

bank.q: Explain the method of joints for a plane truss. Define the degree of static indeterminacy m + r − 2j and explain what happens when it exceeds zero.
outline: Assumptions: pin joints, loads at joints, two-force members
Two equilibrium equations per joint
D = m + r − 2j: zero determinate, positive redundant, negative mechanism
Arrangement must also be stable
Worked truss with all forces; D > 0 needs compatibility
answer: Assumptions. Members are straight and joined by frictionless pins; loads act only at joints; self-weight is neglected or lumped at joints. Each member is then a two-force member carrying pure tension or compression along its axis.
Method of joints. Each joint is a point where concurrent forces meet, so it gives two equations, ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0.

answer.pre:
1. Find the reactions from the whole truss.
2. Start at a joint with at most two unknown member forces.
3. Draw it alone; show each member force pulling away (tension positive).
4. Solve ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0.
5. Move to the next joint, carrying signs. Check at the last joint.

answer: Degree of indeterminacy. With m members, r reaction components and j joints there are m + r unknowns and 2j equations:

answer.pre: D = m + r − 2j

answer: D = 0: determinate, equilibrium gives every force. D > 0: indeterminate to degree D. D < 0: a mechanism. The count is necessary, not sufficient: members crossing without a pin, or reactions that are all parallel, can make a truss with D = 0 move, so the arrangement must be checked too.

answer.text: Worked truss. Pin A and roller B 4 m apart, apex C 2 m above midspan, 10 kN down at C. m = 3, r = 3, j = 3, so D = 0. Reactions 5 kN each. Each rafter makes θ = 45° with AB, so sin θ = cos θ = 0.7071.

answer: When D exceeds zero. Equilibrium leaves D forces free. Each redundant needs one compatibility equation, a statement that members still fit together. For one redundant member with force X, write every force as N = N₀ + Xn and use least work, ∂U/∂X = Σ NnL/(AE) = 0. Three aluminium bars (centre bar 2 m vertical, outer bars at 45°, A = 300 mm²) carrying 50 kN give X = 29.29 kN in the centre bar and 14.64 kN in each outer bar; 29.29 + 2 × 14.64 × 0.7071 = 50.0 kN checks equilibrium.
Closing check. In the determinate truss the joint check at C balances exactly, and in the redundant one equilibrium and compatibility both hold, so each force set is complete.

bank.q: A cantilever beam of length L and constant EI carries a point load W at the free end. Using the unit load method, find the deflection and slope at the free end.
outline: x from the free end: M(x) = −Wx (hogging)
Unit load 1 at the tip: m(x) = −x
Δ = ∫₀ᴸ Mm dx/(EI) = WL³/(3EI)
Unit moment at the tip: m = −1, θ = WL²/(2EI)
Numbers: W = 10 kN, L = 2 m, EI = 2000 kN·m²
answer: Set-up. Measure x from the free end towards the fixed end, and take sagging moments as positive. The load W at the tip bends the cantilever hogging, so the real moment is M(x) = −Wx.
Deflection. Remove W and apply a unit load 1 downward at the tip. Its moment is m(x) = −x. The unit load formula gives

answer.pre:
Δ = ∫₀ᴸ M m dx/(EI) = ∫₀ᴸ (−Wx)(−x) dx/(EI)
  = (W/EI) × [x³/3]₀ᴸ = WL³/(3EI)

answer: The product Mm is positive, so the deflection is in the direction of the unit load, downward.
Slope. Apply a unit moment of 1 at the tip in the sense in which the tip turns under W. It produces a constant moment m(x) = −1 (hogging) along the beam:

answer.pre: θ = ∫₀ᴸ (−Wx)(−1) dx/(EI) = (W/EI) × [x²/2]₀ᴸ = WL²/(2EI)

answer: Again the sign is positive, so the tip rotates in the sense of the unit moment.

answer.text: Numbers. W = 10 kN, L = 2 m, EI = 2000 kN·m².

answer: Units. With kN and metres, M in kN·m, m in m per kN (or 1 for the unit moment), EI in kN·m²: Δ in metres and θ in radians.
Why the unit load sits at the tip. The method equates the work of the unit load, 1 × Δ, with the internal work. A unit load elsewhere measures the deflection at that other point.
Closing check. By Castigliano, U = W²L³/(6EI), dU/dW = WL³/(3EI), the same as the unit load answer. The ratio Δ/θ = 2L/3 = 1.333 m, and 0.01333/0.0100 = 1.333 m, which also checks.

bank.q: A simply supported beam of span L carries a uniformly distributed load w per unit length. Find the central deflection by the unit load method.
outline: Reactions wL/2 each
M(x) = wLx/2 − wx²/2
Unit load at midspan: m(x) = x/2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ L/2
By symmetry Δ = 2∫₀<sup>L/2</sup> Mm dx/(EI)
Result 5wL⁴/(384EI); numbers
answer: Real loads. Span L, load w, constant EI. By symmetry each reaction is wL/2. With x from the left support and sagging positive,

answer.pre: M(x) = wLx/2 − wx²/2        (0 ≤ x ≤ L)

answer: Unit load. Remove w and put 1 downward at midspan. Each reaction is ½, so for the left half
m changes form at midspan, so the integral must be split there. Both diagrams are symmetric, so the right half gives the same value as the left.

answer.text: Integral.
answer.pre:
Δ = 2 ∫₀<sup>L/2</sup> (wLx/2 − wx²/2)(x/2) dx/(EI)
  = (w/2EI) ∫₀<sup>L/2</sup> (Lx² − x³) dx
  = (w/2EI) [L(L/2)³/3 − (L/2)⁴/4]
  = (w/2EI) [L⁴/24 − L⁴/64]
  = (w/2EI) × 5L⁴/192 = 5wL⁴/(384EI)

answer: Mm is positive throughout, so the deflection is downward, in the direction of the unit load.

answer.text: Numbers. w = 3 kN/m, L = 6 m, EI = 5000 kN·m².

answer: Common slip. Writing m(x) = x/2 over the whole span. Beyond midspan m = (L − x)/2; using x/2 there gives a wrong, larger answer. Splitting at the unit load, or using symmetry, avoids this.
Closing check. The standard result 5wL⁴/(384EI) = 5 × 3 × 1296/(384 × 5000) = 19 440/1 920 000 = 0.010125 m agrees with the integral, and the deflection is a small fraction of the span (1/593).

bank.q: A pin-jointed steel truss of m members and j joints carries given joint loads. Explain step by step how you would compute the vertical deflection of a chosen joint by the unit load method, including a tabular layout.
outline: Check determinacy D = m + r − 2j
Real member forces N by the method of joints
Unit load at the chosen joint, member forces n
Table: L, A, N, n, nNL/A; sum and divide by E
Units, sign of the answer, worked truss
answer: Step 1. Check the truss. Count D = m + r − 2j and check the arrangement. For D = 0 equilibrium gives every force; for D > 0 first find the redundants by compatibility.
Step 2. Real forces N. Find the reactions, then solve joint by joint, tension positive, starting where only two forces are unknown.

Step 3. Unit load forces n. Remove all real loads. Put a load of 1 at the chosen joint, vertical (downward if the downward deflection is wanted). Solve the truss again for n. For a linear truss loaded at that same joint only, n = N/P.
Step 4. Table. One row per member, with L in m, A in m², N in N and n dimensionless. Form nNL/A in N/m. If E is the same for every member, sum and divide by E once.
Step 5. Answer. Δ = Σ nNL/(AE). Positive means the joint moves in the direction of the unit load. A zero-force member stays in the table with a zero product.

answer.text: Worked truss. Pin A and roller B 4 m apart, apex C 2 m above midspan, 10 kN down at C; steel, every member A = 400 mm², E = 200 GPa. Wanted: vertical deflection of C. Here D = 3 + 3 − 6 = 0.

answer.pre: Δ<sub>C</sub> = Σ nNL/(AE) = 9.571 × 10⁷ / (200 × 10⁹) = 4.79 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.479 mm downward

answer: Same table, horizontal movement of B. A horizontal unit load at B gives n = +1 in AB and zero in the rafters, so ΔB = 1 × 5000 × 4/(4 × 10⁻⁴ × 200 × 10⁹) = 0.25 mm, the stretch of the bottom chord.

Checks before trusting the sum. (1) Signs: compression negative in both N and n. (2) Units: N and m throughout, A in m², E in Pa. (3) Every member present. (4) Order of size: the deflection should be a small fraction of a millimetre to a few millimetres for a steel truss of this size; 0.479 mm over a 4 m span is 1/8350.
Closing check. By Castigliano, Δ = Σ N(∂N/∂P)L/(AE) with ∂N/∂P = n, which is the same sum, 0.479 mm.

bank.q: A propped cantilever of span L with constant EI carries a UDL w over the whole span. Using the redundant reaction method with energy, find the prop reaction and the fixing moment.
outline: Release the prop; its reaction R is the redundant
Deflection at the prop from w: wL⁴/(8EI) down
Deflection from R: RL³/(3EI) up
Compatibility gives R = 3wL/8
Fixing moment wL²/8, peak sagging 9wL²/128, numbers
answer: Degree of indeterminacy. The fixed end A gives three reactions and the prop B one: four unknowns against three equilibrium equations, so one redundant. Take the prop reaction R (upward) as the redundant.
Primary structure. Remove the prop. A cantilever fixed at A remains, carrying w.

answer.text: Deflection of B from the load. With s measured from B, M = −ws²/2 and a unit upward load at B gives m = s. By the unit load integral:
answer.pre: Δ<sub>load</sub> = ∫₀ᴸ (−ws²/2)(s) ds/(EI) = −wL⁴/(8EI)   (downward)

answer.text: Deflection of B from R.
answer.pre: δ₁₁ = ∫₀ᴸ s × s ds/(EI) = L³/(3EI) per unit R   (upward)

answer.text: Compatibility. The prop does not move:
answer.pre: −wL⁴/(8EI) + R L³/(3EI) = 0     so     R = 3wL/8

answer: The same equation follows from least work: U = ∫(Rs − ws²/2)² ds/(2EI) and ∂U/∂R = 0.

answer.text: Equilibrium.
answer.pre:
R<sub>A</sub> = wL − 3wL/8 = 5wL/8
M<sub>A</sub> = wL²/2 − RL = wL²/2 − 3wL²/8 = wL²/8   (hogging)

answer: Bending moment along the beam. From A, M(x) = −wL²/8 + 5wLx/8 − wx²/2. Shear is zero at x = 5L/8, where M = 9wL²/128 sagging. M = 0 at x = L/4 from A (contraflexure).

answer.text: Numbers. L = 4 m, w = 6 kN/m.

head: Quantity
Formula
Value
rows: Peak sagging, at 2.5 m from A

answer: Common error. Taking the peak sagging moment as RA²/(2w) = 18.75 kN·m forgets the fixing moment. The correct value is 18.75 − 12 = 6.75 kN·m.
Closing check. R + RA = 24 kN = wL. Moments about A: 24 × 2 − 9 × 4 = 12 kN·m = MA. The deflection terms balance: wL⁴/(8EI) = 192/EI and RL³/(3EI) = 9 × 64/(3EI) = 192/EI.

bank.q: A continuous beam has two equal spans L, each carrying a UDL w, with the ends simply supported. Apply Clapeyron’s three-moment equation to find the support moments.
outline: State the equation with the free-moment areas
Simple ends: M<sub>A</sub> = M<sub>C</sub> = 0
Free moment diagram: parabola, area wL³/12, centroid at L/2
Right side −(wL³ + wL³)/4; solve M<sub>B</sub> = −wL²/8
Reactions, sagging peak and numbers
answer: Equation. For supports A, B, C with spans L₁ and L₂, constant EI and no settlement:

answer.pre: M<sub>A</sub> L₁ + 2M<sub>B</sub>(L₁ + L₂) + M<sub>C</sub> L₂ = −6(A₁x̄₁/L₁ + A₂x̄₂/L₂)

answer: A₁, A₂ are the areas of the free (simply supported) bending moment diagrams; x̄₁ is measured from A and x̄₂ from C.
Free moment diagram. A simple span under UDL has a parabola of height wL²/8. Its area is (2/3) × L × wL²/8 = wL³/12 and its centroid is at L/2. So 6Ax̄/L = 6 × (wL³/12) × (L/2)/L = wL³/4.

answer.text: Solving. With L₁ = L₂ = L, MA = MC = 0:
answer.pre:
2M<sub>B</sub>(2L) = −(wL³/4 + wL³/4) = −wL³/2
4L M<sub>B</sub> = −wL³/2
M<sub>B</sub> = −wL²/8   (hogging)

answer: Reactions. Span AB as a free body: RA = wL/2 + MB/L = wL/2 − wL/8 = 3wL/8. By symmetry RC = 3wL/8, so RB = 2wL − 6wL/8 = 10wL/8 = 5wL/4.
Sagging moment. In span AB, M(x) = 3wLx/8 − wx²/2, largest at x = 3L/8 with value 9wL²/128.

answer.text: Numbers. L = 5 m, w = 10 kN/m.

answer: Why the middle support takes so much. Each span behaves like a propped cantilever fixed at B, because symmetry stops the beam from rotating there. That is why MB = wL²/8, the propped cantilever fixing moment, and why RB is 62.5 % of the total load.
Closing check. Total load 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 kN = 18.75 + 62.5 + 18.75. Moments about B for span AB: 18.75 × 5 − 10 × 25/2 = −31.25 kN·m = MB.

bank.q: A continuous beam ABC has spans AB = 6 m and BC = 4 m, constant EI, simple supports at A, B and C, and point loads of 40 kN at the middle of AB and 30 kN at the middle of BC. Solve for the support moments by moment distribution and sketch the bending moment diagram.
outline: Stiffness with pinned far ends k = 3EI/L, distribution factors
Propped fixed end moments 3PL/16 (or PL/8 then release A and C)
Balance joint B; no carry-over to pinned ends
Final moments, reactions, sagging values
Bending moment diagram with values and contraflexure
answer: Stiffness. A and C are simple ends, so for members BA and BC the far end is pinned and k = 3EI/L:

answer.pre:
k<sub>BA</sub> = 3EI/6 = 0.5EI/m      k<sub>BC</sub> = 3EI/4 = 0.75EI/m      Σk = 1.25EI/m
DF<sub>BA</sub> = 0.5/1.25 = 0.40      DF<sub>BC</sub> = 0.75/1.25 = 0.60

answer: Fixed end moments. With the far end pinned, the end moment at B of a span with a central load is 3PL/16. Clockwise on a member end is positive.
(Starting from fixed-fixed values PL/8 = 30 and 15 kN·m, releasing A and C and carrying half over to B gives the same 45 and 22.5.)

answer.text: Distribution table.

answer: One balance finishes the job because nothing is carried to the pinned ends. M<sub>B</sub> = 36 kN·m hogging.

answer.text: Reactions. Each span as a free body with 36 kN·m hogging at B:
answer.pre:
R<sub>A</sub> = 40/2 − 36/6 = 14 kN      B from AB = 20 + 6 = 26 kN
R<sub>C</sub> = 30/2 − 36/4 = 6 kN       B from BC = 15 + 9 = 24 kN
R<sub>B</sub> = 50 kN; check 14 + 50 + 6 = 70 kN = 40 + 30

answer.text: Moments for the diagram.
Sketch. The free moment triangles (60 and 30 kN·m at the loads) are drawn dashed; the hogging moment at B is subtracted along a straight line, leaving the final diagram.

svg.aria: Two-span beam A to C with supports at 0, 6 and 10 metres, 40 kN at 3 m and 30 kN at 8 m. Below, the bending moment diagram: sagging 42 kN·m under the 40 kN load, hogging 36 kN·m at B, sagging 12 kN·m under the 30 kN load, with dashed free moment triangles of 60 and 30 and contraflexure points at 4.62 m and 7.5 m.

answer: Check by three moments. 2MB(6 + 4) = −(3 × 40 × 36 + 3 × 30 × 16)/8 = −720, so MB = −36 kN·m, the same as the distribution.
Closing check. Under the 40 kN load, 60 − 36/2 = 42 kN·m; under the 30 kN load, 30 − 36/2 = 12 kN·m. The final moments at B are equal and opposite, +36 and −36, so the joint is in balance.

bank.q: A torque tube is fixed at one end, and a bracket fixed at right angles to its free end carries a load at its tip. Write the total strain energy of the assembly and use Castigliano’s theorem to find the deflection at the bracket tip. Take a steel tube 1.2 m long, 50 mm outside and 40 mm inside diameter, a solid steel bracket 0.3 m long and 20 mm diameter, a 500 N tip load perpendicular to both, E = 200 GPa and G = 80 GPa.
outline: Tube: bending M = Px and torque T = Pa
Bracket: bending M = Py
U = ∫M²/(2EI) + T²L/(2GJ) + bracket term
Δ = ∂U/∂P term by term
Section properties and numbers; which term dominates
answer: Loads in each part. Let P act at the bracket tip, a = 0.3 m from the tube axis, perpendicular to the plane of tube and bracket. The bracket is a cantilever from the tube end: with y from its tip, M = Py. The tube carries the same P as a shear force, so with x from its free end it bends with M = Px, and it is twisted by T = Pa along its whole length L = 1.2 m.

answer.text: Total strain energy. Shear strain energy is neglected.
answer.pre:
U = ∫₀ᴸ (Px)² dx/(2EI<sub>t</sub>) + (Pa)²L/(2GJ) + ∫₀ᵃ (Py)² dy/(2EI<sub>b</sub>)
  = P²L³/(6EI<sub>t</sub>) + P²a²L/(2GJ) + P²a³/(6EI<sub>b</sub>)

answer.text: Castigliano.
answer.pre: Δ = ∂U/∂P = PL³/(3EI<sub>t</sub>) + Pa²L/(GJ) + Pa³/(3EI<sub>b</sub>)

answer: Each term is the tip movement caused by one action: tube bending, tube twist turned into movement by the arm a, and bracket bending.

answer.text: Section properties.
Terms.

answer: Energy check. U = ½PΔ = ½ × 500 × 0.01268 = 3.17 J, the same as the sum of the three energy terms.

Stresses, as a sanity check. Tube root bending stress 500 × 1.2 × 0.025/(1.811 × 10⁻⁷) = 82.8 MPa; tube shear stress 150 × 0.025/(3.623 × 10⁻⁷) = 10.4 MPa; bracket root stress 150 × 0.010/(7.854 × 10⁻⁹) = 191 MPa. All are elastic for a steel of 250 MPa yield or more, so the linear theory holds.

Reading the result. Tube bending gives 63 % of the movement because the tube is long. To stiffen the assembly most cheaply, enlarge the tube; to cut the bracket term, stiffen the short bracket. Each energy term adds independently because the three actions are uncoupled in a straight tube and arm.
Closing check. Each term has the form P × length³/(stiffness): units N·m³/(N·m²) = m. The total 12.68 mm is reasonable for a light 1.2 m assembly under 500 N.

bank.q: Compare Castigliano’s theorem and the unit load method for finding deflections. Show that one follows from the other, and discuss when each is more convenient.
outline: Both need linear elasticity and small deflections
Castigliano: differentiate U with respect to a load
Differentiating under the integral gives ∂M/∂P = m, the unit load moment
Same numbers on a truss and a beam
When each is more convenient
answer: The two statements.

answer.pre:
Castigliano:   Δ = ∂U/∂P,  U = ∫M² dx/(2EI) + ΣN²L/(2AE)
Unit load:     Δ = ∫Mm dx/(EI) + ΣnNL/(AE)

answer: Castigliano starts from energy; the unit load method starts from virtual work (external virtual work of a unit load equals internal virtual work).

answer.text: One follows from the other. For a linear structure the moment at any section is a sum of contributions from each load, so M = M₀ + Pm, where m is the moment caused by a load of 1 where P acts. Differentiating under the integral:
answer.pre: ∂U/∂P = ∫ M (∂M/∂P) dx/(EI) = ∫ M m dx/(EI)

answer: That is the unit load formula. The same step for a truss gives ∂N/∂P = n and Δ = ΣnNL/(AE). If no real load acts at the point, a dummy load Q is added and set to zero after differentiating, which is the same as applying a unit load separately.

answer.text: Same numbers both ways.

head: Case
Castigliano
Unit load
Answer
rows: Two-bar truss, 10 kN at apex, AE = 1.4 × 10⁷ N
3 m cantilever, w = 4 kN/m, EI = 2400 kN·m²
unit load at tip, m = x
2 m cantilever, 1 kN tip load, EI = 1.6 × 10⁶ N·m²

answer: Common ground. Both need Hooke’s law and small deflections; both give the deflection at one point in one direction per calculation; both handle stepped members by splitting the integral or sum; both carry axial, bending and torsion terms side by side.

When Castigliano is more convenient. (1) When a load already acts at the point, U can be written once and differentiated with no second analysis. (2) For a closed-form symbolic answer, such as PL³/(3EI). (3) For redundant structures through least work, ∂U/∂X = 0, which gives compatibility directly.

When the unit load method is more convenient. (1) When the deflection is wanted at a point with no load: one unit load analysis replaces the dummy-load bookkeeping. (2) For trusses with many members: two force analyses and one table. (3) For temperature change or lack of fit: the real member extension simply replaces NL/(AE), while Castigliano needs extra terms. (4) For many deflections under one load case: the real forces are found once and only n changes.
Closing check. In every row of the table the two methods give the same number, because the derivative ∂M/∂P is the unit-load moment m. The choice is a matter of bookkeeping, not accuracy.

bank.q: A continuous beam over three spans is to be analysed. Compare the three-moment equation and the moment distribution method for accuracy, effort and suitability for hand calculation, and state clearly which you would choose for four spans or more.
outline: Three-moment: one equation per interior support, solved together, exact
Moment distribution: iterative joint balancing, converges
Worked three-span beam both ways, same answer
Effort, variable EI, settlement, fixed ends, frames
Recommendation for four or more spans with reasons
answer: Test beam. Three equal spans AB, BC, CD of 4 m, simple supports at A and D, constant EI, w = 10 kN/m on all spans.

answer.text: Three-moment equation. MA = MD = 0. For a UDL span 6Ax̄/L = wL³/4 = 160.
answer.pre:
Supports A,B,C:  2M<sub>B</sub>(4 + 4) + 4M<sub>C</sub> = −(160 + 160) = −320
Supports B,C,D:  4M<sub>B</sub> + 2M<sub>C</sub>(4 + 4) = −320
Symmetry M<sub>B</sub> = M<sub>C</sub>:  20M<sub>B</sub> = −320,  M<sub>B</sub> = M<sub>C</sub> = −16 kN·m

answer: Two equations, solved exactly: −16 kN·m = −wL²/10.

answer.text: Moment distribution. At B: kBA = 3EI/4 = 0.75 (A pinned), kBC = 4EI/4 = 1.0 (C held). DFBA = 0.429, DFBC = 0.571; the same at C. FEM: BA +20, BC −13.33, CB +13.33, CD −20.

answer: Each cycle cuts the error to 0.286 of the last; six cycles reach 16.00 kN·m to two decimals. (Using the symmetric-span stiffness 2EI/L for BC gives the answer in one balance: DF 0.6, 20 − 6.67 × 0.6 = 16.0.)

Accuracy. Both are exact for elastic beams. The three-moment result is exact at once; moment distribution converges to it and is stopped when the carry-over is small, which is accurate enough for design.

Effort. For n interior supports the three-moment method gives n simultaneous equations. Two or three are easy by hand; beyond that the elimination grows quickly and one slip spoils every moment. Moment distribution needs only additions and multiplications by fixed factors, with joint sums as a running check.

Other features. Three-moment handles settlement and different EI per span by adding terms; a fixed end needs a zero-length imaginary span. Moment distribution takes different EI through the stiffnesses, fixed ends naturally (they are never released), and extends to frames, including sway with an extra step.

Recommendation for four spans or more. Choose moment distribution. Four spans mean three simultaneous equations by the three-moment route, five spans four. Moment distribution grows only by a column per joint, converges in a few cycles, checks itself at every joint, and shows which spans attract moment. Use the three-moment equation for two or three spans, or as an independent check of one support moment.
Closing check. End reactions RA = 20 − 16/4 = 16 kN, RB = 24 + 20 = 44 kN; 2 × 16 + 2 × 44 = 120 kN = 3 × 40 kN. Both methods give MB = MC = −16 kN·m.

bank.q: A truss has one redundant member. Explain how you would find its force using strain energy and compatibility, and evaluate how the choice of which member to call redundant affects the work done.
outline: D = m + r − 2j = 1
Cut the redundant; N = N₀ + Xn for every member
Least work: ∂U/∂X = ΣNnL/(AE) = 0
Worked three-bar truss with two different redundants
Choice changes arithmetic, not the answer
answer: Count. First confirm one redundant: D = m + r − 2j = 1, with a stable arrangement.

Method. Choose a member as redundant and call its tension X. Cut it; the rest is determinate. Solve the cut truss twice: under the real loads (forces N₀) and under a pair of unit pulls at the cut (forces n, with n = 1 in the redundant). By superposition every member force is N = N₀ + Xn.

answer.text: Compatibility from energy. The two faces of the cut must not separate. By least work (Castigliano applied to X):
answer.pre:
U = Σ N²L/(2AE)
∂U/∂X = Σ (N₀ + Xn) n L/(AE) = 0
X = −Σ N₀nL/(AE) / Σ n²L/(AE)

answer: The numerator is the gap the real loads open at the cut; the denominator is the gap a unit X closes.

answer.text: Worked truss. Three aluminium bars hang a pin D: the middle one vertical, 2 m; the outer ones at 45°, 2.828 m. A = 300 mm², E = 70 GPa, load P = 50 kN at D. m = 3, j = 4, r = 6, so D = 1.
Same forces either way.
answer.pre:
Choice 1: middle 29.29 kN, outer 14.64 kN each
Choice 2: outer 14.64 kN each, middle 50 − 1.4142 × 14.64 = 29.29 kN
Deflection of D = 29 289 × 2/(2.1 × 10⁷) = 2.79 mm

answer: How the choice affects the work. (1) The final forces do not depend on the choice: the compatibility condition is the same physical fact written about a different cut. (2) The arithmetic does. Choosing the middle bar kept the cut truss symmetric, so both outer bars had the same N₀ and n and there was one term to differentiate twice. Choosing an outer bar broke the symmetry and needed the horizontal equilibrium equation as well. (3) The cut truss must stay stable: a member whose removal turns the rest into a mechanism cannot be chosen. (4) For hand work, choose the redundant that leaves a symmetric or simple determinate truss, with as few members carrying n ≠ 0 as possible, since only those enter the sums.

Closing check. Equilibrium at D: 29.29 + 2 × 14.64 × 0.7071 = 50.0 kN. Compatibility: the outer bars stretch 14 645 × 2.828/(2.1 × 10⁷) = 1.97 mm = 2.79 × cos 45°, the share of D’s movement along them.

glossary.def: Energy absorbed by a body as it deforms elastically, recoverable on unloading.
The area above the load-deflection curve; for a linear elastic material it equals the strain energy.
The product EI, resisting bending of a beam.
The product GJ, resisting twist of a shaft.
The product AE, resisting axial stretch of a bar.
Work done by a virtual force system moving through real displacements, or the reverse.
A load of magnitude one applied in the direction of the displacement being sought.
Plot of bending moment along a member, used inside the energy integrals.
Moment in a span as if it were simply supported, used with the three-moment equation.
Moment developed at a clamped support of a single span under a given load.
Structure whose support reactions and member forces follow from equilibrium alone.
Structure with more unknowns than equilibrium equations, requiring compatibility.
Condition that displacements at a point must match the restraints actually present.
An extra reaction or member force that is removed to make the structure determinate.
For linear elastic structures, effects of separate loads add directly.
Member loaded only at its ends by pins, so its force acts along its axis.
Truss member carrying no force under the given load case, identified at a joint by inspection.
Pin connection where truss members meet and where equilibrium is written.
The moment needed to rotate a member end through one radian: 4EI/L with the far end fixed, 3EI/L with it pinned.
Fraction of an unbalanced joint moment assigned to one member.
Moment induced at the far end of a member when the near end is rotated.
Lateral joint translation in a frame or truss that adds extra unknowns.
Bending moment at a continuous beam support, negative for hogging.
A load applied at a point, as opposed to a distributed load.
